evals.prompt: Define Porter's Five Forces in 2-3 sentences. Name all five forces and explain what the framework diagnoses.
expected_elements: Names rivalry among existing competitors
Names threat of new entrants
Names bargaining power of suppliers
Names bargaining power of buyers
Names threat of substitutes
Explains industry structure or profit-pool pressure

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model of Five Forces. Name at least 7 primitives and describe how they connect.
expected_elements: At least 7 of: industry boundary, buyers, suppliers, entrants, substitutes, rivals, structural drivers, profit pool, value capture, time horizon
Explains direct rivalry is only one force
Explains forces affect profitability
Explains force strength depends on structural drivers

evals.prompt: Why does this skill exist for agents? Name the failure modes it prevents.
expected_elements: Prevents market-size-only analysis
Prevents direct-competitor-only analysis
Prevents unexplained force labels
Prevents confusing firm strengths with industry structure
Replaces generic market prose with profit-pool diagnosis

evals.prompt: Distinguish Five Forces from Playing to Win, Seven Powers, SWOT/TOWS, PESTEL, and market sizing. Give a mechanism-level reason each neighbor is different.
expected_elements: Playing to Win formulates integrated strategy choices
Seven Powers classifies durable moat sources
SWOT/TOWS inventories internal and external factors
PESTEL scans macro-environment forces
Market sizing estimates demand or revenue potential
Five Forces diagnoses industry structure and profit pressure

evals.prompt: List the ordered workflow taught by the skill, then identify which steps catch over-broad industry definitions, force-label checklists, and static snapshots.
expected_elements: Define the industry boundary
Diagnose each force
Score force strength with evidence
Explain profit-pool effect
Assess trend direction or time horizon
Translate into strategic implications
Over-broad definitions caught by industry-boundary step
Force-label checklists caught by structural-driver and evidence steps
Static snapshots caught by trend/time-horizon step

evals.prompt: Give an analogy for Five Forces that preserves industry-level profit pressure. Then name one bad analogy and explain what it gets wrong.
expected_elements: Uses an analogy with pressure, forces, or value leakage around an industry
Maps multiple external actors to the pressure on profits
Explains the firm is not the only object of analysis
Rejects a bad analogy that reduces Five Forces to a competitor list or SWOT

evals.prompt: Novel scenario: A company wants to enter the online education market because demand is growing. Apply Five Forces by defining a better industry boundary, diagnosing likely force pressures, labeling assumptions, and naming strategy implications.
expected_elements: Narrows online education into a specific category, segment, geography, or value-chain stage
Analyzes all five forces or explicitly notes evidence gaps
Names structural drivers, not just labels
Connects force pressure to profitability
Labels assumptions instead of inventing certainty
Identifies at least one strategic implication
